section_1.title: The Turbulence Puzzle: Defining the Chaos
section_1.content: Introduce the challenge of characterizing chaotic fluid motion. Explain the concept of the Reynolds Number (Re = uL/ν) as the governing ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces. Prerequisite: Basic fluid kinematics.
section_1.example: A trout (the character 'Finley') swimming upstream—show how its wake shifts from a smooth laminar flow to chaotic eddies as it speeds up.

section_2.title: Kolmogorov’s Hypothesis: The Energy Cascade
section_2.content: Explain the concept of 'Energy Cascade' where energy is injected at large scales and dissipates at small scales. Introduce the Kolmogorov 5/3 law: E(k) ∝ ε^(2/3) k^(-5/3). Use an animation of a large whirlpool breaking into smaller vortices.
section_2.example: A large storm cloud breaking down into localized, smaller swirling gusts that eventually fade into heat.

section_3.title: The Kolmogorov Constant (C_K)
section_3.content: Identify C_K as a universal constant in the inertial range of turbulence. Explain that despite local chaos, there is a statistical 'mathematical structure' that is scale-invariant. Visual: A spectral energy density plot showing the -5/3 slope.
section_3.example: Comparing the turbulence of ocean waves with the turbulence of atmospheric jets; despite scale differences, they obey the same power-law structure.

section_4.title: Dissipation Scales: Where Constants Meet Reality
section_4.content: Introduce the Kolmogorov length scale (η). This is where viscosity dominates, and the kinetic energy is converted into internal thermal energy. Explain the transition from inertial range (universal) to dissipation range (specific).
section_4.example: An 'energy-meter' character measuring the size of swirls; as the swirls shrink to size 'η', the energy bar drops to zero as it turns into heat.

section_5.title: Synthesis and Summary
section_5.content: Summarize how constants like C_K allow engineers to model complex flows (like jet engines or weather patterns) without tracking every individual particle. Conclusion: Turbulence is random in motion, but ordered in its statistical laws.
section_5.example: A flight simulator screen showing how computer algorithms use these constants to predict air turbulence around a virtual wing.
